subsubtopic: U.A.R.-ISRAEL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON BORDER SITUATION
speechtext: I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he can report to the house on the situation on the border between the United Arab Republic and Israel which, according to the press, is deteriorating and bids fair to become alarming.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: U.A.R.-ISRAEL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON BORDER SITUATION
speechtext:
The Leader of the Opposition gave notice of his intention to ask this question. We have noted with some concern the reports of troop concentrations and similar developments along the borders between Israel and the United Arab Republic. Although there have been no actual armed clashes in the last few days, one cannot altogether exclude the possibility of a worsening of the situation. I think, however, the latest events, as so often in the past, are due in large measure to the apprehensions which each side has of the other's intentions.
I know the Leader of the Opposition will join with me in expressing a cautious hope that if reason and cool judgment prevail, the present difficulties can be surmounted. I do not think I can go further than express that hope and trust that the situation will not worsen but will be alleviated.

subsubtopic: U.A.R.-ISRAEL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON BORDER SITUATION
speechtext: I wish to ask the Prime Minister a question supplementary to that asked by the Leader of the Opposition earlier this morning on the orders of the day with regard to the dangerous situation in the Sinai peninsula. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister. speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: INTERPROVINCIAL BRIDGE, OTTAWA  REPORTED READINESS OF ONTARIO TO PARTICIPATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not notice that dispatch, but I would say that conversations have been taking place between the premier of Ontario and myself in this regard. He has stated that the province of Ontario would be prepared to provide a share of the cost. I

have also been in communication with the premier of Quebec, who has taken the same attitude.

I was saying, sir, when the hon. member gave us this interesting interlude, that I think the public will be greatly disappointed with the unconstructive attitude of the minister. He seemed to be trying to prove two contrary theses, the one that unemployment was not serious and the other that it had always been serious. Now, I do not think myself that either of these theses was proved, or that this doctrine was advanced at all by the arguments which the minister presented.

speechtext:
I intend to go on in just that way. I should like to remind the committee of what the minister said on Wednesday last. As found at page 1404 of Hansard he said:
There has been a great deal of talk to the effect that unemployment is something that has just happened recently, that it is something that has been brought about since the Conservative government came into office. Let us look at the picture; let us go back and look at what the dominion bureau of statistics figures show.
That, sir, is precisely what I am going to do. I am going to do this because I think if we look at the whole picture, and not just bits and pieces of that picture, we will see that there is something new about the present situation. I do not deny, and nobody in his senses would deny, that there is always some unemployment, that everyone who is able and willing to work is not employed all the time. But what I am going to show, and I think successfully, is that after the war until 1958
Supply-Labour
there was in fact a situation in which there was no continuing problem of unemployment, except a seasonal problem; and I concede that there were a few years in which that seasonal problem was the cause of anxiety.
I am going to say something about that, too, but I do say that from the beginning of 1958 up to and including the present time there have been two new elements in the problem that were not there before. There is the continued high level of unemployment in the summer months, and there is a very much more serious accentuation of unemployment in certain regions of the country. It is just not good enough, as the speech from the throne did, to refer to this as "the recurring problem of seasonal unemployment". If it were only that, even though it might be much more serious than it had been before, it would not be as serious as in fact it is.
Before the minister published the last lot of figures he edified the public by appearing on the television program, "The Nation's Business", on February 4. I might say, sir, that his script was the kind that we are accustomed to from the Prime Minister but which we had never had before from the Minister of Labour; and I do not think it was worthy of the minister, because we are accustomed to feel in the house that the minister does pay some attention to these problems and does take them seriously and make some effort to find out whether what he is saying is accurate before he says it.
This was a document, a propaganda sheet, carefully calculated to give an impression quite different from the impression that all the facts would give. In that speech the minister said, as found on page 2 of the text I have here:
We piloted-
I would draw your attention to this.
We piloted this country through a recession-
Through, mind you, sir.
-which represented a high point in the climbing cycle of unemployment which has been evident since the early postwar period.
I do not know precisely what that high-flown language means, but I do know what the first phrase, "We piloted this country through a recession" means. In other words, and the minister said this specifically elsewhere, he said the recession is over. I have been reminded that, as found at the top of page 2, the minister said, "Today the recession is over". I am coming back to that again, but both in the house the other day and on television the minister went back to 1936 and in the house, as found at pages 1404 and 1405, he gave a lot of figures and said:
Let us look at the situation back in 1936 when the hon. member and his government were in office.

Supply-Labour
He was referring to the hon. member for Essex East.
I am not going to look at any figures released by the dominion bureau of statistics for a time when unemployment is at its peak, which is in February or March. Let us look at the figure in June.
Why did he look at the figure in June? I will tell you, sir. I asked him a question just after that. I asked him if the basis of these figures was the same as it is now, and the minister said that he did not know but he assumed it was. Of course it was not, and any minister of labour who had been minister for three years of unemployment should have known that it was not. This sampling process was only started in 1945, and those figures for the depression period were arrived at by an entirely different process that is described in releases issued by the dominion bureau of statistics, which one would have assumed that any minister of labour would have read.
But notwithstanding that I am quite prepared to admit that a statistical retrospective attempt was made to make these things comparable, and with the permission of the committee I should like to put the figures on Hansard for the whole period. These figures are as at June 1 or the nearest date thereto, and cover the whole period from 1931 to 1959. These are figures taken from the Canadian Statistical Review, and next to each figure is given the percentage of the labour force unemployed in each year. If I could have the permission of the committee and thus save the committee's time by not having to read them I should like, when I have finished using the document, to have it inserted in Hansard at this point.

I should like to draw the committee's attention to the fact that this document shows that from June 1, 1931 through every June 1 until 1936, the percentage of the labour force unemployed never fell below 11.6. On June 1, 1933 it was 19.3. Then in the years after the change of government in 1935 there was a gradual, although very disappointing, diminution. One must remember two things. speechtext: Then you were partly responsible for the depression?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF CORRESPONDENCE WITH MANITOBA

Yes, I would say we were partly responsible, or at least my predecessors were, because I had no connection whatever with that government. I was not even in Ottawa at that time. I did not come to Ottawa until the figures began markedly to improve. I do not suggest there was any connection between those two events although, as a matter of fact, there was probably as much connection-and in my opinion more-as there is between certain events and the claims made by some hon. gentlemen now sitting on the treasury benches.
What I am saying is this, Mr. Chairman. Another thing that has to be remembered is this. The problem in the maritimes is rendered more difficult because of the fact that not everyone is young or strong enough to work in the woods in the winter. I was visiting a camp there three weeks ago. It was interesting to watch the men return to the camp at supper time, about six o'clock,

You must realize that these men receive only $4 a cord, and at the end of a day they have only earned $10 or $12 in some cases. Out of their wages they must feed a horse, pay board and buy gas and oil for the chain saw. There is a tendency now to establish cabins at the camp site and many men have their families with them, and this is an added cost.
While I was in the woods I went to one jobber and asked him if there were abuses in the unemployment insurance system. He said that it depended on how you looked at it, that the odd fellow would come to you and point out that because the cut of wood would be finished in about a month's time he would prefer to be laid off then in order that he could go out and line up another job. This means that the man who has the contract will get wood cut, in any event. There is no question but that the work will be completed. Sometimes the odd little abuse is bound to creep in, but we cannot for one moment curtail or deny benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act because there happens to be the odd abuse. These benefits provide food for the families of unemployed workers. I often complained when I sat in the opposition-and I have increased my complaints since I have been on this side of the house-that unemployment insurance payments should cover all people who are out of work for as long as work is unavailable, because a family keeps on eating whether or not a worker has unemployment insurance stamps in his book.
One matter that bothers me greatly is that one man will have only 14 stamps and will be denied unemployment insurance benefits, but another who has 15 or more stamps will receive payments. Often a man will have only 14 stamps because there were no jobs available to him in connection with which he would receive these stamps. He may have been busy picking potatoes, and no stamps are given for that. He may have been cutting lumber on his own lot to sell to the pulp mills, and no stamps are given for that. He may have been engaged in other work for which no stamps were given. And when winter comes with deep snow he is faced with a situation in which he must watch his children walk to school without breakfast.

I am not able, nor do I intend to try, to compete with the previous speaker either in voice or emotion. I am very grateful that the opportunity has been granted to me to speak on the issue which is now before us, primarily the winter works program but which by unanimous consent of the house has been enlarged to a discussion of the problem of unemployment.
It is a strange but extraordinary fact, Mr. Chairman, that before men and women are nominated, or after they are nominated, they are the most wonderful people in the world, but once they are elected they are damned if they do and they are damned if they do not. For some reason or other, for a long time there has been developing the psychology of running down the status of parliament and of the members of parliament. I was therefore most happy to read the reaction of editorial writers and columnists to a recent and continuing debate in this house on the issue of capital punishment. The discussion and reaction, in my estimation, have done more than anything else in many years to bring the position of parliament and of members of parliament back to where it rightfully belongs.
This is my introduction to the question now before us. I think it would have been, and it would be now, a great thing if we had been able to discuss the problem of unemployment on the same basis and with the same result as we discussed the other matter because, important as the other matter is, this one is even more important.
I have no intention whatsoever, Mr. Chairman, of saying anything on charges and countercharges as between the government

Supply-Labour
and the official opposition on the responsibility for the problem. I have no intention, Mr. Chairman, of saying anything whatsoever on recriminations between the government and the official opposition on this matter, nor of saying one word about the private feud between two Conservative members in this House of Commons. I want to deal with this question of unemployment.
I fully understand the approach of the Minister of Labour in the speech he made the last time this matter was under discussion. Naturally I understand that he, in his position on behalf of the government, puts up the best face possible. We also understand- I do, anyway-the pride he takes in the fact that when one compares the statistics of today with those of a year ago he finds there are more employed today than there were a year ago. But, Mr. Chairman, we have to take into consideration the normal increase in our population in Canada and the immigration into Canada. As prideful as the minister can be, and should be, over the increased employment, this increase as shown in statistics cannot help, nor mean anything to, the hundreds of thousands of unemployed today.
Sir, I am not going to bicker, as some of my friends in the official opposition do so much of, over numbers. I am concerned with the unemployed, irrespective of their numbers, and their numbers admittedly are very large. May I draw the attention of hon. members to something which has been ignored or evaded; namely the basic principle. The government supports free enterprise; the official opposition supports free enterprise. I think this is a moot and an honest question to put. Have they ever tried to answer to their own conscience as to why it is that under the system which they support Canada throughout its entire history has had full employment only when men and women were in uniform dying for Canada, when goods were produced in Canada for destruction; but when men and women want to live in Canada and have goods produced for use, we have unemployment?
There, sir, we have the greatest indictment of the economic system itself and of the individuals and parties that support the system. The record is conclusive, as I am certain the Minister of Labour will admit on reflection. It is a record of prosperity and full employment in war and insecurity for many in peace. No matter what the actual figure is, I will accept the Minister of Labour's own figure. The fact is that we are facing a serious unemployment situation today. Will the minister explain to the house and the people of Canada why we can mobilize completely to oppose an enemy off our shores,

but cannot mobilize completely to deal with the enemy of unemployment within our country?
I believe the hon. member for Essex East put it in slightly different words not too long ago. I say, that if there were an enemy force of 800,000 off our shores we would immediately mobilize completely to counteract that force and defeat the enemy. At a time of need in our own country why cannot the government, having the same authority and responsibility, mobilize all resources to defeat the enemy within our country?
In my estimation the problem of unemployment must be approached from two angles. We have first the short range or immediate situation, and then long range planning so as to ultimately win a victory over unemployment. Without question the short range situation is serious. I do not have the latest figures, but in the Globe and Mail of February 12 I read that jobless fund payments were up 86 per cent at the year end, and that payments from November through December increased from $17J million to $32J million. The situation is worse today.
It is indeed unfortunate-why, I do not know-that in this critical period of unemployment, seasonal if you want to call it that, the situation should have been made tougher for some of those who are now unemployed by the regulations. I have reference, of course, to the two matters that have now been referred by the Minister of Labour to the unemployment insurance advisory committee. But by way of illustration let me add another example involving our Canadian seamen, who sometimes have to work seven days a week and are entitled to overtime pay. They are not paid their overtime pay on board ship, but get it when the ship docks. They also get their holiday pay when the ship docks. I was absolutely amazed when I discovered that in British Columbia, seamen from ships laid up for the winter season cannot get unemployment insurance benefits because the holiday and overtime pay they earned on board ship are being regarded as payments at the termination of employment. I know of no situation involving any other category of workers where that sort of thing has taken place. That is adding to the number of difficulties. We will have more to say about that when the main estimates are being considered.	.
But I want to emphasize this fact. The Minister of Labour admits that there is a serious situation. There are hundreds of thousands of unemployed, many of whom are not entitled to benefits. I believe that the immediate responsibility of the government,

either of its own volition or in co-operation with the provinces, is to make sure that nobody in this country goes hungry at this time, and that they do not lose their homes and personal effects. Never since the hungry thirties have I had so many visits from unemployed in Vancouver and in Ottawa, so many telephone calls in Vancouver and so many letters since I arrived here. Never since the hungry thirties have there been so many who have not been employed for months and who are having to sell their personal effects in order to eat, who are having to sell their homes in order to take care of their families. I say that since the hungry thirties I have not had so many calls and letters as I have been receiving in the last two months and am still receiving.
I say to the Minister of Labour and the government that they must be aware of the situation. All we are asking them to do is to utilize their power immediately, as they would against a foreign enemy, to deal with this vicious situation which is prevalent in Canada today and protect these people until long range plans can be put into effect. The government should protect the personal property and homes of these people so they will have sufficient at least to get by.
I ask the Minister of Labour whether that is not a reasonable request. I ask the Minister of Labour if that is not something he should be doing now, because people are suffering and are losing what it has taken them years to acquire. They cannot retain their homes and personal property because the mortgage and credit companies are taking possession. That is all I want to say about immediate planning requirements, because I do not know now I can add anything else.
But, Mr. Chairman, the main thing is long range planning to attack the continuing problem of unemployment. Let us not call it seasonal or unseasonal. We have always had the unemployed with us under the present and previous governments. From November through March we have always had this problem. Long range planning is required. I am very sorry to have to say this, but I think it is the absolute truth and has got to be said. The Conservatives now are no different from the Liberals before or the Conservatives before that. Their attitude to unemployment is still wishful thinking. What the Conservative government is doing today is the same that was done in the hungry thirties. In their view things will pick up in the spring; prosperity is around the corner.

Yes; an industrial council. I was back in the United Kingdom only this last fall and was in the town where I was born. Ten years ago, in 1949, it was a small place called Harlow. Last fall old Harlow was still there, but there was new Harlow, ten times as large, as a result of planning by government, industry and labour.
Can we not give some thought to that type of planning? Why should Fernie, where the government knew for a year every coal mine was going to close, be left on its own? Why should Tsable river, where we know the last coal mine is going to close-and Tsable river is only a few miles from the city of Cumberland-be left on its own? Why is

Supply-Labour
it that these situations arise? They arise because there has been no planning, but just waiting and hoping for the best, and that things will work out.
In our highly industrialized and competitive economy we cannot resort to wishful thinking. We cannot just hope that things will work out for the best. We are now living in a scientific and a planning world. We ask whether this fact will not be accepted by the government. Changes have been made with regard to unemployment insurance, and that is an excellent thing. The winter works program is excellent in making some provision for 40,000 or 80,000 men. But we are not touching the continuing problem of unemployment.
Is it not time, Mr. Chairman, if we call ourselves responsible members of parliament, irrespective of party, that a different course be followed? If the Conservatives say they are a responsible government, is it not time that this question no longer be left to wishful thinking and haphazard legislation, action or contribution? The government supports agriculture in certain fields if it is in difficulties. The government supports the coal mines in the maritimes under certain circumstances when they are in difficulties. Year after year the government supports the gold mining industry if it is in difficulties. If that principle is correct, why should there not be a plan to keep industry operating in other fields of endeavour in order to keep men and women employed? If that plan was worked out on a national basis, under national planning, I personally feel that it would not cost too much money because of what could be saved from the unemployment insurance fund and what could be gained under the various taxes, direct and indirect. I feel that what is good for one area of the economy is good for the others, if it is done on a planned basis.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that there are two things that must be done today. There must be emergency action in the field of unemployment and there must be planning on a long term basis. I am going to ask the Minister of Labour and the government if they will not face up to realities. I could say "face up to the failures of the past" but I am one who prefers to look to the future. The past is now behind us but the future is ahead. Can we not now face up to the realities, learn from the lessons of the past and really plan for the future in order to conquer this enemy, unemployment?
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I am going to say this to the government with its majority, its promises and what it says is its idealism. You will stand indicted-and up to now you

do stand indicted-in that you are prepared to mobilize Canada with its natural and human resources for war, but you will not do so for the people who want to live and work for Canada. We can say these things, Mr. Chairman, but unfortunately we have not the power to do anything. All we can do is tell the government that we feel they should do these things. If they will at least try, as far as I am concerned they are going to have wholehearted, 100 per cent support and cooperation.
We as members of parliament, no matter where we sit, stand indicted when we have this unemployment situation as it is today and are not taking care of it. Let us face up to this issue so this can be said. I am just going to use the words I used when I concluded my speech in the external affairs debate. Let us by our thinking and by our action, as 265 men and women in parliament who by our thinking and our voting control the laws and the policies of Canada, face up to this issue so it can be said "we pass on to those who come after us a heritage that is greater and fuller because it passed through our hands".

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it was not my intention to participate in this debate on the supplementary estimates of the Department of Labour. In my opinion the debate has already been far too extended, and much of the discussion which has taken place on this item could well have taken place when the regular estimates were presented to the house. My reason for rising is that there have been speakers in this debate who have brought in the potential unemployment at Elliot Lake, and at the same time they have brought in the question of the new nuclear research establishment at Whiteshell, which is in my constituency. Some have suggested that it would be in the interests of employment at Elliot Lake that this project be transferred to that place.
It is not my intention at this time to go into a debate upon the situation in the uranium industry and atomic research field in Canada. In the few remarks I have to make I am going to refer to the unemployment situation as it exists in Elliot Lake, and I would like to show this house that the relocation of this project could not in any way relieve that situation. During the past few days I have contained myself when I have listened to speakers in this house, when I have read about the speeches made in the Ontario legislature, when I have read the many press reports, when I have seen the splashes on television, and when I have listened to the misconceptions regarding this nuclear research centre.

First of all, before proceeding to that topic I might say that this government admits the seriousness of the unemployment situation, and we admit our concern about it. However, I notice that the dominion bureau of statistics weekly bulletin of February 19 states that there were 161,000 more people employed at mid-January this year than at the same time last year. It also states that the number of people seeking employment is 34,000 less this year than at the same period last year. Surely then, Mr. Chairman, the situation is not quite as black as has been presented in this house by some speakers in the opposition.
More particularly this item has to do with the winter works program, and may I say that in my constituency many of the municipalities have not taken advantage of some of the provisions of this item. However, we have had one or two instances where it has added to employment in my area, and I feel that as long as this measure is going to do something to alleviate the seasonal unemployment situation during the winter months, then it should have the unqualified support of all hon. members of this house.
On October 1, 1959 the Minister of Trade and Commerce announced at a press conference in Winnipeg that because the research facilities at Chalk River had expanded to the point where no further expansion was warranted at that establishment, it was desirable to establish a second research centre for Canada. He announced at that time that because of the fact that Manitoba lacked any major federal research project, that nuclear research establishment would be located in Manitoba. Atomic Energy of Canada officials investigated various sites in Manitoba, and on January 19 it was announced by Atomic Energy of Canada that the new nuclear research centre would be located at Whiteshell, 60 miles north east of Winnipeg on the Winnipeg river near the town of Lac du Bonnet.
The reasons for the choice of this site were purely technical. First of all, the site had to be located on a river with ample water flow. Second, it had to have a firm bedrock to bear the heavy weight of the facilities which were to be put in. Third, it had to be close to a university. The decision that was made by Atomic Energy of Canada was an impartial decision, and it bore no political implications. I read in the Winnipeg Tribune of February 23 the following:
John Fullerton, member of the Ontario legislature for the riding containing Elliot Lake, has said he will resign his seat if it is found that the Diefenbaker government's decision to establish the nuclear plant in Manitoba was based on a "petty political consideration".
Supply-Labour
Mr. Chairman, I think the facts show that there were no petty political considerations in the choice of this area, and that indeed the hon. member who represents Elliot Lake in the Ontario legislature need not resign. In fact, if this government were to give in to the organized pressure that has been brought to bear on it to change the location of the site it would indeed then be considered petty politics, and in that case perhaps the hon. member for Springfield would have more reason than the hon. member for Elliot Lake for resigning.
Before proceeding to the unemployment situation at Elliot Lake I would like to say something about the projected employment that this nuclear research establishment will provide for Manitoba. First of all it has been stated that no work or construction will take place on the actual plant until after the spring of 1961. Atomic Energy of Canada officials have predicted that the first reactor should go into operation late in 1963 and more likely in 1964, and that at that time a staff of 200 people would be employed at the research establishment.
May I call it one o'clock.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at one o'clock
I had just established why the nuclear research establishment was placed in Manitoba, and I was going on to give a projection of the amount of employment it would create in the foreseeable future.
Officials of Atomic Energy of Canada have stated that no construction will begin on the plant site until after the spring of 1961, the reason being that first of all access roads have to be put in and a bridge has to be built across the Winnipeg river. I am hoping that the federal government in co-operation with the provincial government may see fit to provide some winter employment on the clearance of these roadways and of the plant site itself. In late 1963 or 1964 it is expected that the first reactor will go into operation in Manitoba, and at that time it is expected that a staff of 200 will be required to man this reactor. Let us remember that the people who will be staffing this reactor will be for the most part technicians, and certainly the opening of this reactor will not

Supply-Labour
provide too many jobs for the type of people who are unemployed at Elliot Lake. A further projection is that by 1970 perhaps 1,000 people will be employed at Whiteshell.
I want hon. members to remember these figures because I will return to them when we consider the situation at Elliot Lake. The question I want to bring up at present is where would more employment be created as a result of this nuclear project-in Manitoba or at Elliot Lake? First of all we must remember that there is no town site at Whiteshell and therefore a good many more jobs would be created because of the need to construct homes for the employees. At Elliot Lake there is an established town site, and far less employment would therefore be created in this respect. In my area and on the prairies as a whole we know that there is a shrinking population in relation to the rest of Canada and part of that shrinkage has been due to the fact that there has been no opportunity for the young people of the west to remain at home. I know that as I go through my own constituency I see very few young people, because as soon as they are out of school they are sent abroad to find opportunity elsewhere. There has no doubt been a great export of brains and intelligence from the prairies. In fact, we can look around this house and see evidence of it right here. I am thinking in particular of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. I am sure that the people of the maritimes would have been very happy if this new nuclear research project had been created many years ago so that the hon. member could have stayed in his native province.
This year has been a very bad one for the people of Manitoba and of my area in particular, because their crops were almost wiped out. We must remember that the people who settled the prairies after the Canadian Pacific railway was built were hard-working people who were settled on marginal land and who, with nothing but their fortitude and their faith in the future, have carved out their fortunes in the granite on the edge of the preCambrian shield. These people certainly deserve consideration.
I should like to turn for a moment to consider the situation at Elliot Lake. Here is a community of 25,000 people, and it is estimated that some 9,000 are employed in the mines. According to the Financial Post of February 20 it is expected that in 1961 some 3,500 will have lost their jobs and that by 1963 the number of unemployed will have risen to 5,000, and by 1966 to 7,500. I am not as pessimistic as these figures. I fail to see, however, that if this Whiteshell nuclear project is transferred to Elliot Lake it would be

of any immediate help, because it would be 1965 before the project came into operation and at that time only 200 would be employed on the staff. Also, as I said, those 200 would be technicians.
Let us consider the structure of the town of Elliot Lake. There are 2,337 permanent homes and 463 multiple dwellings in the area. The planners designed Elliot Lake for a population of 12,000 and an optimum employment force of 5,000. That is what they anticipated, but this boom town which is bursting at the seams now has a population of 25,000 people. I do not think the cut-back in employment is going to do a great deal of harm to homeowners because there are 5,000 families at Elliot Lake who are living in trailers. It is no great hardship for those people in trailer homes to hitch their homes behind their cars and go to places where there is more opportunity. Besides, there are 210 families living in basement apartments, and that is not suitable accommodation. I understand, also, that many people with homes are renting rooms to people who cannot find accommodation.
I do not believe that Elliot Lake will become a ghost town. It will probably remain as its planners had originally designed it, with a population of about 12,000 and a working force of about 5,000. Why is it that the opposition have suddenly pounced on this nuclear research centre going to Manitoba to cure all their ills in Ontario? I should like to quote from an article which appeared in the Ottawa Journal on February 19, 1960:
Speaking in the throne speech debate. Mr. Wardrope-
The minister of reforms in Ontario. I continue:
-said the government is negotiating with industries that will eventually employ 15,000 men.
Further along in the same article Mr. Wardrope is reported as saying:
-the new industries will use natural gas and iron ore. Mining developments in the "foreseeable future" will mean 100,000 new citizens for the north, he added.
And again, further along in the same article:
The two plants near Nakina might create a town of 10,000 residents in three or four years, he said. It was hoped they would hire 1,500 next year.
Surely actions such as these are more conducive to alleviating the unemployment situation in Elliot Lake. In view of the action the provincial government is taking I should like to quote from an editorial which appeared in the Globe and Mail on February 25, 1960:
The problems of Elliot Lake are not going to be solved by performances like that of the opposition in the Ontario legislature on Tuesday. The

resolution which Liberal leader Wintermeyer tried to bring in was, by his own frank admission, out of order. It proposed that the legislature petition the dominion government to give Elliot Lake the nuclear research station planned for Manitoba.
Mr. Wintermeyer's action in bringing it in, and the conduct of the Liberal and C.C.F. members during the disorderly debate which followed, suggested that they were not interested primarily in helping Elliot Lake, but in making a political football out of it.
Further along the editorial states:
Asked in Tuesday's debate for a statement of his own government's position on Elliot Lake, Premier Frost answered, "We are pressing in an orderly way for a solution of the problem". This is the right approach. It would best be implemented by one or more non-political conferences attended by men of practical experience in the social-industrial-economic problem Elliot Lake presents. Queen's Park should be working to bring such discussions about.
I feel that is the right attitude to take toward the problem in Elliot Lake. Yet, when the provincial Liberal leader's resolution was ruled out of order his own comment, as reported in the Ottawa Citizen of February 25, was:
The federal government is either playing "elementary politics" or does not know what is happening at Elliot Lake, Mr. Wintermeyer said.
I would suggest that the leader of the Liberal party in Ontario is the one who does not know what is going on at Elliot Lake and at Whiteshell.

speechtext: What about the provincial member, Mr. Fullerton?

speechtext:
If the hon. member for Essex East had been in the committee before one o'clock he would know that I had already dealt with that. There has been a lot of talk on television and in the newspapers and much plain exaggeration. I heard one report to the effect that 1,000 telegrams had been sent to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I personally investigated and learned that only 40 odd telegrams had been sent to the minister. There was a strange thing about those telegrams in that they all asked that the Whiteshell nuclear research establishment be moved to Elliot Lake. Surely that smacks of organized hypocrisy. But the people of Elliot Lake are not the only ones who sent telegrams. I have also received a few.
I wish to illustrate the difference in attitude between the people of Ontario and the people of Manitoba. I should like to place on record a resolution passed by the rural municipality of Springfield in February of this year. I understand that a copy of this resolution was forwarded to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce in the form of a telegram. The resolution reads as follows:
Supply-Labour
Resolution was passed by the council of the rural municipality of Springfield in Manitoba in which they expressed sympathy with the conditions which are coming into existence in Elliot Lake, Ontario, with the slowdown in uranium production. However, it is felt that the need in Manitoba for a project of the magnitude of the new nuclear research station in the Whiteshell area is a long-standing need. It is urged that the government do everything in its power to keep the project from being taken from Manitoba.
The people of Manitoba are not trying to take anything away from anybody but sympathize with the position in Elliot Lake. I have already demonstrated that taking this nuclear research establishment away from Manitoba certainly would not solve the unemployment situation at Elliot Lake. I am proud of the people of Springfield and of Manitoba in general who sent me telegrams couched in language that reflects an attitude different from that of the people of Ontario who wired the minister to the effect that this was petty politics and that the research establishment should be taken from Manitoba and placed at Elliot Lake.
Let us look at the record in Ontario. Ontario is one of the privileged provinces. The government has centred nearly all its nuclear research centres in that province. During the last 16 years the federal government has spent $120 million in this field in Ontario. Ontario has the four major reactor projects the two at Chalk River and the new one under construction. There is also CANDU, a $60 million project. I am surprised that the Leader of the Opposition has ceased asking that this project be transferred to Blind River or Elliot Lake. On July 9, 1959, as reported at page 5704 of Hansard, the Leader of the Opposition directed the following question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce:
A supplementary question. Does the minister not realize that the perfect site for this power reactor would be the Blind River area, where there is lots of water, lots of rock and lots of uranium?
I believe the Leader of the Opposition asked the same question on January 21, 1960 as reported at page 166 of Hansard for this session. But why the sudden silence? Why not put on more pressure with respect to the project that is slated for Ontario requesting that it be relocated at Elliot Lake if it is really thought that this will solve the situation at Elliot Lake? Certainly that would be much more fair to the people of the country as a whole if one project in Ontario were transferred to another site. I am not suggesting that this be done but I do ask the question, why pick on Manitoba? Is it because the Liberal party has been wiped out in

Supply-Labour
Manitoba? Certainly action such as this will ensure that the Liberal party will remain in oblivion in that province.
I direct a plea to the Leader of the Opposition on behalf of the provincial Liberals in Manitoba. They are most embarrassed by the attitude their party has taken in this house. To ensure that they are not wiped out provincially, I urge the Leader of the Opposition to change his attitude. I would also suggest that the hon. gentleman apologize to the people of Manitoba for the attitude he has taken. Certainly I hope he will have the courage to come to Manitoba and defend the stand he has taken in this house. I know he will be welcomed in Springfield.

speechtext:
At the conclusion of my remarks.
I have dealt with the factors that reveal that Ontario has enjoyed a privileged position in this field. As I explained before one o'clock, the reasons for placing this research establishment in Mantitoba were sound and logical. No politics or petty considerations were involved and certainly none should be involved in matters such as these.
I read in the newspaper yesterday that 500 women are coming to Ottawa to protest this matter. I then listened to a program on television and heard it stated that 150 women were coming. That statement was made on "Tabloid". Certainly there is an aura of exaggeration about all these things. It was stated that 1,000 telegrams were sent to the minister but I inquired and learned that only 40 were sent. It was stated that 500 women were coming to Ottawa but another report stated that only 150 were coming. I will certainly be on the steps of this building on that occasion to see how many arrive and I believe there will not be even 150.
I heard another interesting statement on "Tabloid" last night. A union leader said that these uranium companies had made a profit of $150 to $160 million. I do not know if that is true but if it is I believe there is an onus on these companies to spend some of their exorbitant profits which they received because of the backing they obtained from this government. They should spend some of this money to assist the people in those areas in this period of potential critical unemployment. Are these companies going to take the attitude that they have no obligation whatever in this respect? It seems to me they should take a different attitude.
I was surprised when Mr. Wintermeyer suggested that the Whiteshell nuclear research establishment should be placed at Elliot Lake.

I was surprised that Mr. Winters should have stated that the placing of the nuclear research establishment at Elliot Lake would create 2,400 jobs. It is apparent from the facts I have stated that this is not the case at all. The fact is that after 15 years the plant at Chalk River employs only 2,400 employees and certainly it will take a much longer time for the same number to be employed at the Whiteshell nuclear research establishment.
I am not quite as pessimistic about the outlook of the uranium industry as some of the members in this committee, Mr. Chairman. I have reason to believe that in future years-in 10 years, or so-the demand for uranium and the supply of uranium will probably come into closer balance. Therefore, there is nothing to indicate that all those uranium towns, not just Elliot Lake but Bancroft and Uranium City, and so on, are going to become ghost towns overnight. I feel that with a sensible program we can do something to alleviate unemployment in those areas and at the same time ensure that there is some continuation of those resources that no doubt will be necessary as time goes on.
It was not my intention to participate in this debate, Mr. Chairman, because I felt it had already taken up too much of the time of the committee. However, I have been so upset over all these allegations, coming as they do from responsible people who should know better, that I could not help but stand up and point out the facts to some hon. members. I am sure that as time goes on the decision of the government will prove to be correct. There is no doubt in my mind that the nuclear research establishment at White-shell will continue and I hope it will do a great deal to expand the economy of that part of the country and provide opportunity for our bright young people at universities, raise the standards of our scientific faculties at those universities and do something to decentralize the concentration of industry and of research and place it in other parts of the country which need it much more badly than Ontario.

Mr. Chairman, listening to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), Tuesday, February 9, when he gave us certain explanations concerning this item, we did not have to be great psychologists to see that he was quite uncomfortable; he must realize, as we do, that the winter works program offered by the government to provinces and municipalities is altogether inadequate.
Then again this week-it was Wednesday afternoon-speaking in this house he proved clearly, I thought-and the minister might perhaps reread his speech-that not only is this government altogether unable to solve the unemployment problem but does not seem particularly concerned over the ever growing number of unemployed.
To hear the Minister of Labour talk, the government finds quite normal, it seems, that there were more than 800,000 unemployed in December and in January.
The government feels there is no reason to make a fuss about this because, as I said, this is considered normal.
The government seems to think that, by providing a winter works program, it has done its duty and kept all its pledges in this respect. Furthermore, the government seems to suggest that it is up to the municipalities to solve this problem, because indeed it is the municipalities that have to pay more than 90 per cent of those works. I say more than 90 per cent, Mr. Chairman, because this fact can be supported by figures. Last winter, for instance, according to figures provided by the Minister of Labour himself, $6.5 million were paid over to municipalities for such works, out of a total of $50 million spent this way. Actually this would put the federal government's share at 13 per cent. But, on the other hand, we must not overlook that, out of the 87 per cent that remains to be paid on that winter works program, municipalities have to borrow money at 7, 7J, 7J and even sometimes 7.89 per cent. Furthermore, when municipalities have to get their plans prepared by engineers, again they have to pay a further 7 per cent of the costs of 79951-0-95i
Supply-Labour
such works. But the government pays no part of that interest that the municipalities have to pay, nor of the additional 7 per cent that they have to pay to the engineers who draw up the plans for those projects.
Under the circumstances, it can therefore fairly be said that municipalities today have to pay over 90 per cent of the costs of those projects. Yet, it will be remembered that, at the time our hon. friends were sitting on this side of the house, and during the 1957 and 1958 elections they claimed they could handle that problem. I don't think a single member of the Conservative party sitting in this house can deny that, during the elections, he stated, as did his leader, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), that nobody, not a single Canadian, would suffer from unemployment while the Conservative government was in office.
Well, Mr. Chairman, what is the position today? And it has been the same since 1957. The situation has not changed: there are 750,000 to 800,000 unemployed in Canada. I wonder what the government has done to solve this problem.
No wonder, as stated the other day by my colleague, the hon. member for St. Denis (Mr. Denis), that only about 60 municipalities out of a total of 1,600 in the province of Quebec, took advantage of this winter works program. Yet the Minister of Labour and his colleagues from the province of Quebec know that this province is still the one most severely affected by unemployment, because more than a third of all the unemployed are Quebec people.
I hope the minister will not pretend to believe that in Quebec city, for instance, where there are now 17,000 people out of jobs, the problem can be solved simply by half a million dollars worth of winter works. You know that last year, municipal authorities there undertook works for a similar amount and, according to a Quebec city alderman, that amount of $400,000 or $450,000 could provide jobs for no more than about 100 unemployed for two weeks each.
Besides, it is the same thing in Montreal. The other day the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) informed the house that this year, according to figures supplied by the Minister of Labour himself, this winter works program in Canada's metropolis, where there are now 83,000 unemployed, will provide jobs for only 863 people. Imagine the tremendous number of unemployed this will help: only 863 out of 83,000. Besides, the picture is the same in other large cities throughout the province.

Supply-Labour
It seems to me that, after the various representations and suggestions made, and more particularly after two years of experience with that program, when the minister spoke in this house last Wednesday, he could have told us that he was thinking of improving his program. But no; he made a speech that was defeatist and demoralizing not only for hon. members but specially for the 800,000 unemployed we now have in this country.
I am not questioning the minister's sincerity and personally I am convinced that he would like to do more but that he is being prevented from doing so. He realizes that this winter works program is picayune, and inadequate. Of this I have no doubt at all. Indeed, if the minister has read the brief submitted by the Canadian federation of mayors and reeves, he could not help noticing that the submission had mighty little good to say about his winter works program, contrary to what he gave us to understand the other day when the hon. member for St. Denis was dealing with unemployment. I have this brief before me and I may assure you that the program is far from being commended. For the minister's information, I shall quote some excerpts with regard to the winter works program. This is part of the chapter "Municipal winter works program", and I quote:
(Text):
Municipal Winter Works
The municipal governments are strongly of the view and urge that the range and nature of eligible projects under the federal-sponsored municipal winter works program be broadened and extended to include building construction as well as outdoor construction projects, particularly in northern communities where outdoor construction is not economically feasible and in those municipalities where there is a high incidence of workers normally engaged in the construction trade.
Moreover, and inasmuch as some municipalities have been experiencing difficulty in obtaining temporary bank loans in order to finance their share of the costs of a winter works program, the municipalities urge that the federal government request Canadian banks to facilitate, wherever possible, any loan requirements of municipal governments for such projects.

at other times by other members, do in effect a disservice to the maritime provinces. Across the years the maritimes, my own province, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, and now Newfoundland, have had quite an obstacle in the fact that we are more or less on the tail end of the nation; we are cut off from the basic economic centre of Canada. To a certain extent across the years we have seen a substantial decline since confederation in our capacity to produce per capita and generally in our economic potential.
But I would not have hon. members think that the situation in the maritimes is as bad as has been pointed out, or as has been suggested by some members here. Perhaps, part of the reason, part of the difficulty we have had in building up the maritime provinces is to be found in the pessimism and in the bad reputation we are given by some members who stand up in this house, and in other forums, to run down our provinces in the east and to suggest that we are incapable of building up or that our situation is hopeless.
As a matter of fact quite the contrary is true. Across the years we have had our problems. But I want to say to you, Mr. Chairman, and to all the members in this committee, that never before in the history of the maritime provinces have we had the opportunity for advancement that we have today; never before have we had the potential to build that we have now. It certainly does not help our chances or our opportunities to be exaggerating the unemployment figures, to be misinterpreting them, or to be suggesting to the nation that the maritimes is an inappropriate place for investment at this time. This is in effect just what is being done by members who paint too bleak a picture of the maritime provinces.
What are the facts? The facts are that in the last three years there has been a considerable boom in the maritime provinces. In the last three years the problem of industrialization has, at last, been tackled by the governments there and we are seeing now a light in the darkness. The Liberal governments in power in Nova Scotia and at Ottawa during the 23 years before 1956 and 1957 tried with a conspicuous lack of success to do something about the problem of the maritime region. They talked from time to time about trying to assist us to industrialize. In fact, they did nothing. Year after year, in relation to the rest of Canada, our economy declined. Now at last it is beginning to pick up. It certainly does not help us a bit to have people indicating that the provinces in the east do not offer as good opportunities as they did before 1957.
Supply-Labour
After the election of the Stanfield government in Nova Scotia in 1957, for example, there was set up Industrial Estates Limited, which was to assist in providing capital for the attraction of industry and to provide buildings that would be rented at reasonable rentals to industries which would locate there. This is an indication of the action of the government, in general, toward coaxing industry into the province, and to date it has been an outstanding success.
As evidence of this outstanding success during the last three years, I would cite the fact that 14 new industries have been established or revivified in the province of Nova Scotia. That is progress. During all the years the Liberal party was in power my province had only two major manufacturing industries. We had the pulp and paper plant at Liverpool and the steel plant at Sydney both successful. The coal mines were always in trouble since the first world war, except during wartime.
Since 1957 we have had new manufacturing industries in Nova Scotia. I refer, for example, to the establishment of the $40 million pulp mill in my riding, at Point Tupper. This will be the third major manufacturing industry in Nova Scotia and it will give employment to a large number of people, both in the mill and in forest operations. We are looking forward to substantial advancement in Nova Scotia, and the situation is not at all as it has been represented by some speakers here today. I do not suggest we have, as yet, made the progress we would like to make. I do not suggest everything is rosy in the maritime provinces. Of course, these figures on unemployment are serious. But I do say that, for the first time within the memory of people living in my province an attempt is being made to remedy the situation and to find more employment for our people. Certainly this was not the case during the long years the Liberal party was in power in this country.
I spoke of industrialization. We have made an important start on this problem. At the same time we are building a network of highways as good as any in Canada. We are building them at a high rate. In the last three years there have been 800 miles of new paved highway laid in Nova Scotia. This certainly is progress. The very substantial increase we have had, amounting to 200 per cent, in conditional grants from this government has made it possible to substantially improve educational facilities, highway facilities, and so on; all of which will help to build

Supply-Labour
up an economic climate which will provide a remedy for the ills of Nova Scotia and the other maritime provinces.
I spoke of education. For example, in 1959 we had 50 per cent more teachers in training in the normal schools; we had 100 per cent more teachers in training in our colleges. We have new schools being built at a tremendous rate everywhere in Nova Scotia. The other day I heard a prominent journalist from the maritimes comment on the situation. He said the city of Saint John was looking forward to the greatest boom in its history. I believe the same thing is true of Newfoundland. Newfoundland was a very backward province when it came into union. It is being developed very swiftly today. The federal government is co-operating in discovering and marketing the resources of this great province. When Newfoundland's resources and promise are marshalled, it will provide a further great boon to the Atlantic provinces.
Some special mention was made of the unemployment figures for the maritime provinces. It is true, as I have said, that this is a serious situation. I would not have hon. members believe that the situation was such, however, that Nova Scotia would not go ahead and was not a safe place for investment. Actually the unemployment figures are accentuated by three things. First of all, as all hon. members know, seasonal unemployment has always been the bugbear of the eastern provinces. A large part of our resource industries, agriculture, farming and fishing, do not provide employment during the wintertime as they do in the summer. At the same time we have had a very prosperous year in 1959 and a large percentage of the unemployed are drawing unemployment insurance benefits. I think it is well known that in former years, during 1956 and before, there were a good many years when we maritimers faced the problem of seasonal unemployment without unemployment insurance to provide for our people during the winter. That is not so today.
There is another point, unemployment figures might be different, in a way, because of the effect of the new optimism and the new opportunity in the maritime provinces. We have had a change in our labour force. Up until 1957 the Atlantic area lived constantly with the tragedy of our young people leaving to go to the United States, Ontario or Quebec or elsewhere to seek work and a decent living. Now a great many of these young people are staying at home because they know there is new hope in my province and in the other Atlantic provinces. These people swell the labour force.

speechtext: Eleven of them came up here in 1957.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF CORRESPONDENCE WITH MANITOBA
speechtext:
Yes, a good employment opportunity for Nova Scotians.
There has been some talk about the Atlantic resolutions to which maritime members subscribed in 1957. The hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate suggested to you, sir, and to this committee that there has been a complete default on those resolutions; that, in fact, nothing has been done to help the maritime provinces. Nothing could be further from the truth. The spirit and tenor of the Atlantic resolutions has been recognized and accepted and in many respects there has been great fulfilment of these resolutions by this government.
The hon. member spoke of national resources development. I can tell him, for example, of the development of Cape Breton Highlands national park in my constituency. It has been built up tremendously in the last three years, providing much employment while the work was progressing. There has been a resultant increase in the tourist industry in Cape Breton Island. It increased by 39 per cent in 1958, and 17 per cent in 1959. This progress is important. Our tourist industry is building up fast. It is one of our important national resources, and it has been with the assistance and sympathy of this government that our tourist industry has boomed as it has.
The roads to resources program will help to open up new areas, apart altogether from the extra money made available by this government to Nova Scotia to stimulate the tremendous highway program we have had. In so far as national resources are concerned, I might mention the tremendous capital funds that have been provided for the building of wharves, breakwaters and other harbour facilities in the maritime provinces. This has been a tremendous help in improving our most important fishing industry. I daresay the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, if he were honest, would admit that more has been done in his constituency in the last three years toward providing harbour facilities than ever before.
As far as I am concerned my constituents never before saw such expenditures as this government has provided to build up the harbours throughout my constituency. The fishing industry is being stimulated and proving the value of that investment in my riding. The same is true across the rest of the maritime provinces.

As far as decentralization of industry is concerned, we from the maritimes recognize that that is not an easy proposition. We see what happens when attempts are made to decentralize industry across this nation. Current in the news is the question of whether or not the atomic power research centre should go to Manitoba rather than be settled in Ontario. There are always two sides to these questions. Certainly I have yet to see a member from the Liberal party rise in his place and say that research centres and so on should be taken out of the central provinces in order to be established in the maritime provinces or in the western provinces. Usually they take the reverse position.
Speaking of defence contracts, may I say that a large part of the economy of Nova Scotia is dependent on defence contracts. The city of Halifax derives much of its income from the large naval establishment and shipyard there. The new establishment in the valley has been a substantial fulfilment of the promise to locate more defence organizations in the maritimes. Certainly the naval base at Point Edward close to Sydney, which employs 600 men, has been a tremendous boon to the economy of Cape Breton island.
As to power development, may I say this. The power development project which is going ahead rapidly and is providing a good deal of employment will give us cheaper power which will mean a great deal to the development of the maritime provinces. This power development program is being pushed ahead by this government in order to try to assist us in the province of Nova Scotia and in the other provinces.
While I am speaking of this matter I should like to point out to you, Mr. Chairman, that the power development program, as first conceived by the Liberal party, would have been of no value whatever to Nova Scotia without assistance in the way of subventions to bring coal to the power plants. We all remember that only a short time ago the Liberal party in this house, through the then minister of northern affairs and national resources, refused to accept the suggestion of subventions on coal to power plants within Nova Scotia but suggested instead that the high prices of oil which obtained during the Suez crisis showed that coal would be able to compete with oil in those power plants, even though he must have known that coal could never compete with residual oil from abroad without subventions. Those subventions on coal made the power program a reality in Nova Scotia and in New Brunswick and will mean, I hope, that we will have
Supply-Labour
cheaper power. The power program would never have meant cheaper power under the program suggested by the Liberal party in 1956 and 1957.
As to transportation may I say this? One of our greatest problems is transportation, as it has been since 1900. But at the moment the whole problem of transportation is being gone into by this government and we are hopeful that as a result of the inquiry by the royal commission, the inequality under which we suffer will be remedied. We expect that this government, after gathering all the facts, will take measures to improve the transportation cost as it effects the Atlantic provinces. But I say this to you, Mr. Chairman. In all the years that the Liberals were in power they refused even to consider this question. If they criticize us for appointing a royal commission, may I say that at least the government is trying to do what it can to gather the facts fairly, to have all opinions put forward and to come up with a solution to the problem.
Mention has been made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, in his attempt to paint as bleak a picture as possible, of the Atlantic provinces of the coal industry. Yes, Mr. Chairman, we have grave troubles in the coal industry. We have had them for a long time and they are accentuated today by the new competition of oil that comes in through the pipe line and by the natural gas finding its way into our markets in Montreal and along the St. Lawrence river. This is quite a problem. The government has faced up to it squarely and has listened very patiently to all of our proposals in this regard and I know is seeking everywhere for a solution.
The Rand commission we expect will go into this matter very thoroughly and will come up with a long term solution to the coal problem. There is no way of solving it by waving a magic wand. As a matter of fact, this government, in the tremendous subvention assistance it has provided for has made the position of the coal mines very much better than it would have been if the policies of its predecessors in office had been continued. When you consider the fact that last year $13 million in federal subventions went to the province of Nova Scotia-mostly into Pictou county and Cape Breton county-to assist in meeting the problem of the mines, we can all appreciate that this government is doing everything it can to help; and the people at home know it, even though they also realize that the situation is a serious and vexing one.

Supply-Labour
Just in closing, Mr. Chairman, I should like to suggest, as I have suggested before, that the solution to the basic problem of the maritime region or the Atlantic region is not to be found in political headlines and is not to be found in ad hoc programs to partially meet one crisis after another as they come up, as was done through the years under a Liberal administration. We all recognize that the Atlantic region constitutes a special economic problem.
We must have industrialization and it will come only if our industries in the Atlantic provinces are able to compete, to produce goods as cheaply and to sell them as cheaply as do industries located in other areas. It is obvious to anyone that if a man has his choice between locating an industry in the Atlantic provinces or of locating in Ontario or Quebec, he is going to choose the province in which he thinks he can show the greatest profit. I think that what we must do is to equalize opportunity by showing the manufacturer in the Atlantic provinces the same profit as he can realize in the central provinces. How we can do that will have to be studied very carefully. Personally, I believe that the best way in which the problem can be properly solved is by tax concessions which would allow a manufacturer as great an after-tax profit as he would have if he were manufacturing here in Ontario or in the great province of Quebec.
Some mention was made by the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska of the question of tight money as it affects our provinces in the east. I do not think the hon. member was suggesting that the tight money situation as we find it was the result of deliberate policy of this government. However, he pointed out that tight money means one thing in Ontario and Quebec and means an entirely different thing in the Atlantic provinces, To us it means that where money was tight previously, it is now almost impossible to get. I think all must recognize that in the Atlantic region there should not be put into effect policies to check inflation either by the government or other agencies in the country. A definite attempt was made, I think by the chartered banks of Canada, in the interests of controlling inflation, to tighten up money in many areas. I believe it should be pointed out to the men who lend money in this nation that there is no justification for cutting back on loans in the Atlantic provinces in order to control inflation. There is no inflation problem there, although it may exist in other parts of Canada. I would hope that this government
[Mr. MacLeUan.l
would bring to the attention of bankers and agencies throughout that nation the fact that there has never been any reason nor is there at the moment any reason to cut back the money supply in the Atlantic provinces because of the problem of inflation.
