Mr. Chairman, the discussion has been going on for four days with regard to the $15 million earmarked for winter work, and the government has suggested no additional action, no change in policy in respect of the unemployment problem. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), as well as all other members of this government, are entrenched behind their winter program and do not want to see conditions as they are. The sight of
800,000	unemployed is not enough to pierce
Supply-Labour
the fog which hides the earth to all Conservative members who are still in a state of ecstasy after their coming into power in the 1958 election.
In the speech I made on the address in reply, Mr. Chairman, I said that the winter works program was a monumental hoax, and I am if anything more convinced of it today.
In Montreal, the winter works program is practically, if not completely inexistant. Why?
First of all, because the government always decides too late to tell the municipalities whether they will be able to avail themselves of a federal grant with regard to special projects during the winter. Second, the government is putting too many limitations on the work which those municipalities may carry out.
What are the municipal authorities to do, when, during the summer months, they wonder what the government's intentions are with regard to the various winter projects they might undertake?
The government announced last October that the municipalities would be able to benefit from a winter works program. This government should, first of all, understand that, in a city like Montreal, before any reasonable study of such program can be undertaken, plans be established, tenders called for and contracts let, before all this has gone through the usual administrative channels months of work are required. A notice of a few weeks by the federal government will therefore hardly give enough efficiency to the winter works program in Montreal, from the point of view both of the unemployed and of the city.
I said a few moments ago, that the government is putting on too many limitations with regard to the work the municipalities may undertake, and I shall quote a few instances, in order to bolster my argument: Under the winter works program a municipality is not entitled to have any work done by the hydroelectric commission with regard to the lighting of streets, to traffic signals, the various water mains and transformers. Moreover, the city may not do any construction work in its yards, nor erect any buildings. These are just a few facts I have been able to gather, as I had no time to study the consequences of such limitations more thoroughly.
Can you imagine, Mr. Chairman, what the difference would be if the government decided to put no restriction on the types of works the municipalities could undertake?

Supply-Labour
The unemployed would be the first to benefit; municipalities would avail themselves of the opportunity to have certain necessary improvements made, and manufacturers providing the necessary material for those various works would have to keep their staff twelve months a year instead of seven or eight months, as is the case in many factories today.
The government, which keeps asking the opposition what they would do or what they have to suggest to settle this or that problem, will allow me, at this time, to make two very simple suggestions in order that this winter works program may become, if not a success at least a means of providing work, not only to a mere 40,000 persons but perhaps to
150,000	or more during the hard winter months.
This would help decrease the number of jobless people and would undoubtedly spare the Minister of Labour many a headache. It would at the same time allow the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) to fulfil the election promises he made when he said that, so long as he would be Prime Minister, no one would suffer from unemployment. It is not merely one or a few unemployed, that we now have in Canada, but 800,000 of them.
Let the government announce right now, or at least as soon as possible: 1-That municipalities will get grants for winter works next year; 2-That no restrictions will be put on the types of works in which Canadian labour might be employed.
I have here a communique sent to me by the Minister of Labour: it is dated November 20, 1958, and it explains the winter works program. Here is what article 3 says:
Classes of admissible works, subject to each winter works undertaking being accepted, are as follows:
(a) Construction and major reconstruction of streets, sidewalks and highways, except main highways.
In the province of Quebec, Mr. Chairman, it is not possible-and I can say so, even though I am not an engineer-to build streets or sidewalks of the types mentioned in those winter works.
Here is now what the Minister of Labour specified in article (b):
Construction and major reconstruction of water work, sewer and waste-water services.
This is about the only type of work that municipalities like Montreal can undertake during the winter.
Here is what the item says:
Construction and development of municipal parks.

That is the winter works program, those are the only projects that municipalities can undertake throughout Canada to assist 800,000 unemployed registered at present.
This is very limited, and the Minister of Labour, instead of pretending that unemployment is not as serious as it is, that unemployment is not on the increase, should-I conclude here, because I have in my hand a press release from the Department of Labour showing the employment situation in January 1960:
In January, the total of persons employed was estimated at 5,699,000, a decrease of 162,000 compared to January and December.
Within a month, 162,000 more persons had to apply for unemployment insurance, and the Minister of Labour, the Prime Minister and all Conservative members keep on pretending that unemployment is not a problem.
I said it before and I say it again: unemployment is the cause of all the trouble we now have in Canada.
Here is one of the reasons for the figure of
162,000	unemployed. A third of this number were people working on construction, while half of them were employed in trades, in industry, in factories and in agriculture.
Week after week the Minister of Labour gives us the number of unemployed, and we find that it is always on the increase. And day after day the Minister of Labour and the Prime Minister keep repeating on television and elsewhere that the unemployment situation is not serious, that it is not as alarming as members of the opposition would have us believe.
The February 10, 1960 issue of La Presse published an article by Mr. Paul Martel under the heading:
Winter unemployment threatens our national economy.
Allow me to quote only a few sentences:
Winter unemployment is one of the serious problems gnawing at the national economy, Mr. Paul Martel stated this week . ..
Every winter, Mr. Martel added, thousands of workers are laid off and have to go on the dole. This results in a drop in production and a loss of purchasing power estimated in millions of dollars.
This shows, Mr. Chairman, that employment in Canada is related to the whole economic system.
I think I have made a few valid suggestions, and I feel the Minister of Labour should include them in his general winter works program.
It would also be of benefit to every unemployed person in Canada if the Minister of Labour took the time to review his winter

works program with a view to making any amendments required to enable the municipalities to share in it.
In Montreal, for instance, and as a means of providing winter employment, the winter works program might include a subsidy for snow removal, which would allow the municipality to employ manual workers to clear garage entrances, skating rinks and public parks after heavy snowfalls, instead of using blowers. Furthermore, and again as a means of providing employment, manual workers might be employed to clean out the street sand from sewers.
Again as a means of reducing the number of unemployed, an effort might be made to use more manual workers instead of equipment in larger cities, and so on.
Mr. Chairman, I think if the Minister of Labour were sincere and really wanted to correct the present situation, he would put forward new suggestions, so that municipalities might take better advantage of the winter works program.
A few moments ago, I heard the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) tell the house that the mayors of municipalities in his constituency called him up to inquire as to what they might do to benefit from the winter works program. Apparently, he does not wield too much influence in his constituency.
I see on a list I have here that the town of Farnham will get $2,450 from this winter works program. This aid will give work to 15 people for five months. It means that each person will get $163, or $32.60 for one month and $8.15 for a week. I think those people had better apply for relief to the St. Vincent de Paul society in their parish; I am sure they would get much more money.
As far as the province of Prince Edward Island is concerned-and this is even more amusing

there is a project for which the contribution of the federal government will be $250. We must admit that it is quite an amount. This project which will be executed under the winter works program will provide work for 10 people. For a whole province, it is mighty big. It means that each person will get $25 for five months of work. For one month each will receive $5 and for one week each of those ten people of the province of Prince Edward Island will receive $1.25. If it could help the government, I would be quite willing to take one or two of those people and to help them live through the winter with what the government offers them. Frankly, they need much sympathy.
Supply-Labour
So, here is the aid that the government and the Minister of Labour are offering to our 800,000 unemployed. They do nothing. And this program is nothing but a screen behind which they hide while pretending they are doing the utmost to alleviate unemployment. As I said at the beginning, this government and the Minister of Labour are doing nothing to alleviate the misery of our 800,000 unemployed all across Canada.
I conclude these few remarks, Mr. Chairman, by saying it is useless to make suggestions. In fact, this debate is in its fourth day and the government has not yet mentioned that it intends to modify its winter works program. If the government intends to improve it, it keeps perfectly silent about the matter.
In this regard, may I recall the message delivered on New Year's day by the Minister of Labour, which was published in the National Labour Journal. I will not read it all, but only the last two paragraphs. Here is what he said:
As Minister of Labour, I can assure you that I shall do all I can at the federal level to find solutions for our labour problems.
According to the prospects at the beginning of this year, there is every reason to be confident and, through the co-operation of workers, employers and governments, 1960 should be a year of happiness and prosperity for all Canadians.
Mr. Chairman, if things remain the same during 1960, the number of unemployed will continue to grow and this year will not be as happy as forecast by the Minister of Labour in his New Year message. However it is desirable that, around Easter time, after a careful self-examination, and in view of the plight of the 800,000 unemployed across Canada, the Minister of Labour should draft a new message and announce major changes in his winter works program.
Furthermore, let us hope that the Minister of Labour will announce right now whether municipalities may take advantage of this offer next winter and whether the restrictions will be changed, so that in the winter of 1960-61 our unemployed will be better off and their families happier.

Mr. Chairman, this is the third occasion on which I have participated in this debate and although some may feel that three times is too often for one member to speak during the course of a debate I make no apologies whatever for rising at this time to speak about what I consider to be one of the most important problems if indeed not the most important problem to come before us this session.
I should like to confine my remarks today to something that has arisen since the last time I spoke in this debate. I refer to the problem that has recently arisen in the city of Elliot Lake. This was discussed at some length the other night by the Leader of the Opposition. With all due respect to that hon. gentleman for whom I have considerable personal admiration I believe I can safely say that he befogged this problem more than I thought it was possible to do.
The hon. member for Springfield spoke on this subject this afternoon and, I may say, very eloquently, but I am afraid I have to take issue with some of his remarks. The hon. member went on to list some of the reasons why this research centre should be built in Manitoba rather than located at Elliot Lake. If I heard him correctly he gave as one of the reasons the fact that there is bedrock available at Whiteshell such as is needed to support a building of this size. I do not know what type of rock they have in Manitoba but if the hon. member can find more bedrock anywhere in the country outside of the Rocky mountains than he will find around the city of Elliot Lake, I should like to know where it is.
The city of Elliot Lake was practically blasted out of rock. That is one of the big blunders that was made when this community

was built. Within a distance of 5 miles of the present site there is a perfectly level strip of ground that would have served as a wonderful location for this city but the grandiose plans called for the city being located where it is and as a result the taxpayers of Canada will be called upon to pay almost twice the amount they should pay for the construction of buildings in that city.
Another reason given by the hon. member for the location of this research centre at Whiteshell is that it would be near the University of Manitoba. I acknowledge the truth of that statement but I also know that at the present time extensive plans are being made and funds are being raised across northern Ontario for the establishment of a university in that area. The present houses that will stand empty in the city of Elliot Lake would be a wonderful place to start a university. Think of the cost that could be saved if this and projects of a similar nature were moved into the available houses in that city.
I do not know how many hon. members have visited Elliot Lake in the last year or so. For those who have not visited it recently I should like to state that it is probably the most modern up to date city on this continent. There is not a single shack, dead end street or unpaved road or sidewalk in the city. It is likely that the city will become the most modern and up to date ghost town on the North American continent as it was described in a recent newspaper article.
The hon. member for Springfield mentioned the embarrassment of the Liberals in the province of Manitoba. I should like to place on the record a letter I received from a faithful follower of the present government who lives in Elliot Lake which should be a source of embarrassment to the present government. It was written by a business man in that community whom I knew very well in the town of Timmins, having served with him through two terms on the school board of that municipality. This man invested something like $80,000 in a business in Elliot Lake and unless something is done quickly he will lose his investment. This is what he wrote:
I am writing this letter to seek your active support on a matter that is of the utmost importance to all of us in this community. I feel that it is almost equally important to the Canadian taxpayer wherever he may live. That matter is namely the relocation of the proposed atomic research centre at Whiteshell, Manitoba, to the Elliot Lake district. I would like to enumerate only a few of the more important reasons why this is the only sensible thing to do.
1.	This area is a fully developed community with first class facilities of all kinds fully developed to handle the situation with no further expenditure required as against opening a new community in the bush miles from nowhere to cost the taxpayers millions upon millions of dollars.

2.	This community in which both governments have spent millions of dollars faces almost certain complete collapse in 1966 with a loss to the federal government of some $40 million in N.H.A. loans alone. (Wouldn't it be ridiculous to do the same thing all over again in another section of the wilderness?)
3.	This is where the uranium is for any such project. No more need be said about that.
4.	Even with the relocation of the project here it is certain that many of the mines will be closing which would leave beautiful, permanently constructed buildings available for space required by such a project. Without mentioning names I am thinking of one mine in particular that is due to close soon. The buildings there are excellent and there is water over 300 feet deep at their front door.
5.	The energy resources of Ontario are almost fully developed and new sources must be found whereas Manitoba has only scratched the surface. Now. I realize this has little connection with a research centre, but would fall in line with the allied subject of power developed from uranium.
6.	With the people of Manitoba this is a nice thing. An extra to be gained from the government. With us it is a life and death struggle for many who have placed their life savings in the development and future of this community; after all, the money wasted here came partly from the Manitoba taxpayers too.
Nobody in his right mind would object to federal aid to increase property and industry in our good prairie provinces, but this is such a terrible duplication of services and such a waste of millions. The fact that the Whiteshell proposal in the first place could have been a political reward for certain people doesn't enter into this discussion as I am not qualified to remark on it.
You may wonder why a lifelong Conservative would write such a letter to an up and coming C.C.F.'er. Well, I'll tell you. In our past association we usually seemed to be of a mind on most matters; furthermore, I sincerely feel that this whole situation is above party politics. I may remain a Conservative all my life so that you can understand how it pains me to tell you notwithstanding my own affiliation, that I have lost all confidence in this present administration, this matter being only one of the many causes for such feeling on my part.
Murdo, please give this your unreserved consideration and see what you can do in the house.
I think that letter speaks very well for itself, Mr. Chairman.
The hon. member mentioned something he had seen in the newspapers recently about a cabinet minister from Port Arthur in the provincial government, a Mr. Wardrope, who had made a sweeping generalization about how great developments in northern Ontario are going to absorb the people from Elliot Lake. The hon. member for Springfield also pointed out that many of the miners in Elliot Lake would not be qualified to work in this research centre. I would suggest that the same remarks would apply to the development mentioned by Mr. Wardrope, if and when it ever comes about.
But I think this problem points up something that has been overlooked far too much in this debate so far. I certainly realize the
Supply-Labour
importance of the problem so far as the miners who are affected in Elliot Lake are concerned, because I know many of them personally. So far we have completely ignored the businessmen in that town, the men who have gone in there and who have sunk every bit of money they had and every cent they could raise to establish themselves in business. I know the Minister of Trade and Commerce the other night and the hon. member for Springfield today mentioned the fact that possibly in 10 years' time Elliot Lake might be booming again. That is a long time between meals, as far as the people there are concerned. While the hon. member made a very good point that if the research centre was moved to Elliot Lake it would not provide immediate employment, yet it is a fact that if the businessmen in Elliot Lake knew that this research centre was to be established in that community they at least would have some hope in the future. I see no hope at present and neither do they.
I see my time is getting short, Mr. Chairman, and I would like to switch to another matter which has risen just this week and which is affected by but not necessarily contained in the same problem. Many hon. members may have seen a report in the Toronto Star that miners laid off in Elliot Lake were returning to Timmins where they were facing a situation where immigrants are being brought in and given preference in work in the gold mines of Ontario. I have checked my local papers and I see that this allegation is denied by the local mines and, at the same time, people who know the situation say that they have proof of this. At this stage I dc not know whether they are right or wrong. I think the government should look very closely into this situation because if it is true it means that three cabinet ministers are going to be very much embarrassed by this action on the part of the mine operators. First of all, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration will be embarrassed because it is through her good offices that these people must come here. I have nothing whatever against immigration provided provision is made to give the immigrants some opportunities when they get here. But I ask hon. members what kind of reception are we giving immigrants coming into this country when they find themselves in situations such as we have at Timmins at the present time? They would be cursed and reviled the moment they set foot in Canada because they would be taking jobs away from trained miners in the Timmins area. What kind of reception is that? What kind of immigration policy is that?
This action would be embarrassing to the Minister of Labour in his efforts to find a solution to this unemployment problem. It

Supply-Labour
is fine to bring people in, but it you cannot feed your own family you do not invite in your neighbours. And last, but far from least, it will embarrass the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, who has a bill on the order paper to extend the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act for another three years. Of the two mines involved, one is reported to be recruiting 400 immigrants and the other is planning on bringing in 10 families per month. In the 10 years in which the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act has been in force these two mines have received $14,976,270.32 from the Canadian taxpayer.
It has just been drawn to my attention that at the present time there is not one single member of the cabinet in the house to listen to this debate.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. W. Kucherepa (High Park) moved
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-9, respecting the Canadian Public Health Association.
He said: The purpose of this bill is to bring up to date an act respecting the Canadian Public Health Association which was passed in 1912. The Canadian Public Health Association today is a mature, well-balanced association representing the many professions concerned with public health in Canada. Its activities have kept pace with the changing pattern of public health and covers a broad and varied field. The association today might be described as follows.
The association is a national organization with eight provincial branches located across the country. All the provincial branches have the same objectives as the main body. The fact that there are eight provincial or regional chapters does not mean that there is a gap in the country-wide coverage. There are separate chapters for seven of our provinces and New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island are joined together in one regional association.
Which ones?

New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. Newfoundland is not at present connected to any particular provincial or regional arrangement but the public health workers in that province have been active in association affairs.
Public health today covers a broad and ever-expanding field. The membership of this association reflects this pattern by including physicians, dentists, veterinarians, nurses, sanitarians, laboratory personnel, health educators and others, who are making a real contribution to the affairs of the association.
The work of the association is carried out by its members through study groups, continuing and ad hoc committees, and by presentations at the annual meeting of the association. As I mentioned earlier, the association brings together many professions, and each of these, in turn, has its own professional

body. The team concept must be fostered and the committee on needs has recommended that the association establish a much closer link with other professional organizations. At the same time, the association must continue to demonstrate the value that individual members receive from belonging to an organization made up of people in fields of mutual interest. Therefore, a trend in the future is likely to be a closer working relationship with other professional health bodies and a more prominent role for the Canadian Public Health Association within this group.
An important need in Canada, as in most other countries, is a better co-ordination of professional and voluntary health effort. In recent years we have seen a remarkable increase in the number of health agencies. While such increase is evidence both of unmet needs and of an active public concern in meeting these needs, it has resulted in a very complex pattern so that the necessity for co-operation and co-ordination of effort is becoming clearly evident.
As I mentioned earlier, the purpose of this bill is to bring up to date an act respecting the Canadian Public Health Association. For example, this bill will permit flexibility in fixing the place of the head office. The present act fixes the place of the head office as Ottawa. For many years the actual administrative headquarters has been Toronto, and it was thought desirable at this time to make provision to change the head office from Ottawa to Toronto, with power to relocate at some future date if this should appear necessary.
This bill will bring the act up to date by inserting words of modern usage which have developed in the intervening years. The original bill used the word "sanitation" which apparently at that time was considered descriptive of what is now referred to as public health. It was thought appropriate to amend this archaic phraseology and to substitute the more modern expression "public health and preventive medicine". This bill will also clarify and extend the matters which may be dealt with by by-law, such as providing for the establishment of new classes of members which is considered desirable if the association is to keep abreast of developments. It also provides the technical provisions for the calling of meetings; the method to be used in enacting, repealing or amending by-laws; the powers and duties of the officers and other matters which are part of the operation of other associations with not very different aims.
Originally part of the act dealt with the first general meeting of the association. This is being dropped. Another section made
Private Bills
reference to the original incorporation and specified by name the members of the first executive committee. This is also being dropped. The new bill is intended to make provision for an executive council and an executive committee and for representation thereon.
The original act placed a limitation on the quantity or value of real property which the association may hold. This is no longer regarded as necessary or desirable in organizations of this kind, and it was thought desirable that this should be repealed. There would be substituted a new section which would authorize the association to acquire property, real or personal, to borrow money and do other things as are necessary in accordance with modern usage and practice in such activities. The clause in question is one that is in general use. For example, I think it is contained in almost identical language in the act incorporating the Canadian women's press club. I know that all members of the house will agree with me that over the past 48 years this association has made a real contribution to the welfare of Canada.

I should like to say a brief word about this bill which I am sure will be supported by all members in this house. The Canadian Public Health Association has rendered, through its officers and members, such distinguished service in the interests of the health of this nation that the opportunity should not be allowed to pass without acknowledging the great debt everyone in this country owes to the Canadian Public Health Association. This association has developed and spread throughout our country a knowledge of public health and preventive medecine, as well as other matters pertaining to the highest standards of health care which all of our health workers seek and have so successfully effected.
I should like to say to the hon. gentleman who has just spoken that this also affords me an opportunity to say to him what I am sure every hon. member in this house would also say, and that is how grateful we are to him for what he has done in the administration of the Salk vaccine to members of parliament and to public servants quartered in the houses of parliament.
The Canadian Public Health Association has had some distinguished officers administering the organization. As one who had the responsibility of recommending health policy on federal account to my colleagues in government, my own association with this

Private Bills
body was very intimate, just as I am sure the Minister of National Health and Welfare at the moment has a close association.
There are many names that stand out in my mind as I think of this body, but I would want to single out particularly the man who was president of the association when I first became minister of national health and welfare. I should like to use this occasion to acknowledge, on behalf of the Canadian people, the great debt Canada owes Dr. R. D. Defries, the director for such a long period of the Connaught Laboratories and the man who was, perhaps more than any other apart from the research scientists who discovered the Salk vaccine, responsible for making our program in Canada such a great success. Dr. Defries is also remembered, along with the late Dr. Banting and Dr. Best who had so much to do with insulin. The production of insulin at the Connaught Laboratories is linked to Dr. Defries who is as well a great figure in the Canadian Public Health Association. I am sure the house generally will recognize that anything that renders more efficient the operation of a body like this deserves the approval of the house.

In
rising to express the wholehearted support of this party for this bill and the purposes of this very worthy organization I feel like somewhat of an initiate in this field in following two gentlemen who have rendered distinguished service in the health and welfare field. I refer to the hon. member who introduced this bill and to the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). I am glad on this occasion for once to have a kind word to say for him. He was our former minister of national health and welfare and, as everyone knows, he took a great interest in this problem.
I was interested in the hon. member's explanation of the purpose of the bill and the purpose of this organization which, I understand, was commenced about 1912 and whose principal function was to promote a knowledge of public welfare and to promote ideas that would give effect to various services that were required in the areas in which the organization serves. I think that our changing concepts with respect to public health are clearly indicated in the change in wording in this measure. Whereas in the old act the objectives of the association are stated to be:
-the development and diffusion throughout Canada of the knowledge of sanitation in all its branches, and all other matters and things appertaining thereto, or connected therewith.

In this bill those words are changed to the following:
3. The objects of the association shall be the development and diffusion throughout Canada of the knowledge of public health and preventive medicine and all other matters and things appertaining thereto or connected therewith.
Just changing those words clearly indicates, in my opinion, the change in ideas with respect to what public health means today as compared with what it meant in 1912. I know that when I was a small boy public health as far as I was concerned meant cleanliness and washing my neck every morning before going to school. It was largely centred around this idea and was not considered on as broad a scale as it is today. This change in language indicates the broadening scope of this society.
I was interested in the hon. member's description of the work of the society, of its being national in scope, of its having provincial or regional organizations, and of its membership. I was interested to hear him mention that it aimed to promote teamwork amongst the professional persons he mentioned and also teamwork with other health bodies. I was pleased to note that fact because I am under the impression-and I find it in other spheres of human activity-that there is sometimes a tendency for there to be a wasting of effort in overlapping, in duplication and things of that sort. I find that tendency in a good many public activities throughout the country. I am glad to note that he mentioned that there was a particular desire to promote co-ordination and co-operation between voluntary health agencies through the Canadian Public Health Association.
Having made those few brief remarks, Mr. Speaker, I now resume my seat, wishing this organization continued success in the future in the good work it is undertaking for all Canadians.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills.

speakeroldname: Mr. O. W. Weichel (for Mr. Websier) moved

the second reading of Bill No. S-ll, respecting Montreal Life Insurance Company.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount (Mr. Webster), the sponsor of this bill, may I as seconder present it on his behalf.
This bill asks for authorization to change the English name of the company into its corresponding French version, and to use both names, all for the purpose of doing a more extensive business, as this company

expects to do. The bill is a sign of the times and indicates the growing understanding between the two peoples of Canada through the diffusion of the two languages.
Montreal Life Insurance Company arose from the Travellers Life Insurance Company, which was formed by the acts of incorporation and amending acts, June 16, 1908. I understand that business actually began on May 26, 1910, and the name was changed May 27, 1924 to Montreal Insurance Company.
The company issues a complete range of life insurance and annuity policies, both participating and non-participating. It was the first Canadian life insurance company to include disability benefits in its policies and is one of the companies still prepared to grant the monthly income disability benefit.
The past 50 years have been a record of continuous and healthy growth with noteworthy progress in every sphere of operations. The company has enjoyed economical and capable management and its earned rate of interest on investments has for many years been one of the best among life insurance companies operating in Canada.
Montreal Life Insurance Company occupies its own head office building in the city of Montreal and has 25 branch offices throughout Canada, ten of which are in the province of Quebec.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce.

ALGOMA CENTRAL AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-12, respecting the Algoma Central and Hudson Bay Railway Company.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the prime purpose of this bill is to amend the incorporating act

so as to permit the company to operate with greater efficiency. As you will recall, in 1958 the company came to this house with a bill to reorganize and to change its financial structure. As a result of the operations under that act the company now has been able to clear off a trust agreement and for the first time has been able to operate under the direction of its own shareholders.
In their operation they have found that while operating under the Railway Act they are somewhat hampered in administrative detail. For that reason the first committee meeting of the shareholders, after the termination of the trust agreement on March 10, 1959, which was held on April 2, 1959, at which they decided to ask permission of this house to make the amendments set out in this act.
The affect of the amendments will be to provide that the general meetings of the company will be anywhere in Canada instead of being restricted to Sault Ste. Marie. They will be able to increase the number on the board of directors to a maximum of 15, and also to amend the quorum to be not less than four directors; also they will be able to provide for an executive committee. That was done for the Canadian Pacific Railways some years ago. They will also be able to put into effect the principle of alternative directors. They also wish to make it possible to apply to this house, if necessary, for authority to add to their financial structure in a more efficient way than in the past by requiring a vote of 10 per cent of their shareholders instead, as formerly, of two thirds.
That, Mr. Speaker, is roughly the purpose of this bill. The parliamentary agent and the officials of the company will be available when this bill is referred to committee if passed by this house, and I am sure they will give any detailed information which would assist any hon. member concerning the problems of the company.
I might just add a word in case some hon. members are wondering about the object of the alternative directors. Under our own dominion act that is not permissible, but it has been a practice which has grown up in England and adopted by some of the provinces of Canada, such as the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and New Brunswick, and I have the authorities here if any hon. member should require that information. It would mean that because the directors are spread right across not only Canada but sometimes outside Canada, an alternative director would be named to act on their behalf at a directors meeting.

maintopic: ALGOMA CENTRAL AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
Might I ask a question. The hon. gentleman has mentioned about the alternative directors, and I was wondering

about that in my own mind. If there is an executive of four directors out of twelve, how will this operate? How are the alternatives named? Are there alternatives for every director? Perhaps the hon. member would say a word or two more on that, although I realize of course, that the bill will go to a committee where it will be finally determined.

Mr. Speaker, I am not sure of the exact operation this company has in mind, but it was explained to me that there are occasions where a director will be unable to come. In that case an alternative director who, I understand, has been formally approved by the other directors can come and take the place of the director and act during the meeting as if he were a director. But his authority only lasts so long as the director is away.
As to further details I prefer to let the officials of the company explain this so that there will be no misunderstanding as to their operation.

This bill is not completely original as far as I am concerned. I have placed bills on the order paper in the past which would 79951-0-96J
Small Loans Act
have limited the interest rates which could be charged by small loans companies and other lending institutions to a maximum of 12 per cent per year. It has been pointed out, however, in this house on previous occasions, and it has been pointed out to me in private conversations I have had with hon. members of the house and members of the press, that there is a good deal of interest, and it is felt by many a good deal of support, for the idea that small loans companies in advertising their lending facilities should be required to set forth the interest rates that are charged for the loans they make, particularly when they set forth the payment plans.
The first clause of the bill reads as follows:
Section three of the Small Loans Act Is amended by adding thereto the following subsection:
"(5) Whenever a money-lender advertises himself as carrying on the business of money-lending and in such advertising indicates the monthly or other periodic payments required for the payment of any loan, he shall also indicate in such advertising what the total cost of any such loan amounts to in terms of percentum per annum."
There have been a number of similar bills moved by private members in the past which have recommended themselves to hon. members of the house. Even in the field of small loans, by presenting bills asking for a reduction in interest rates and by obtaining for those bills a great deal of public support, private members influenced the government of the day to act in a very commendable way by introducing its own legislation subsequently referred to the banking and commerce committee, reported to the house and passed into law. As a result of that legislation many millions of dollars in interest payments have been saved, in my opinion, to the borrowing public.
Small loans companies are providing larger and larger total amounts of consumer credit in Canada. They are a growing business a business growing in importance. In 1951 small loans companies made loans totalling $114 million; by 1959 the total had increased to some $431 million, an increase in that period of time of more than 200 per cent. Oviously, this is a growing field, a field of growing importance, and in my opinion it is a field in which greater control should be exercised by the parliament of Canada and by the superintendent of insurance.
I can see no disadvantage which would accrue from requiring small loans companies in their advertising and in setting forth their carrying charges to name the interest rates that are charged. I think it is very much in the public interest that this information should be made public and that the borrower

Small Loans Act
who has to go to a small loans company for a loan shoujd walk in with his eyes open as far as interest rates are concerned.
I have in my hand a piece of literature put out by the Household Finance Corporation. It lists the various amounts that may be obtained as loans. It lists the repayment cost per month with regard to these loans, but in no case does the interest rate appear. Perhaps some people who do not take into account the fact that the loans are repaid on a monthly basis may calculate that on a loan of $500, for example, repaid in 12 months with a carrying charge of $56.06 there would be an interest rate of 11 per cent. Of course, that is not the case. The interest rate is roughly twice that amount, since the money is repaid in 12 annual instalments and therefore the person borrowing the money does not have the $500 for the full 12 month period. In this chamber in other years the former member for Saskatoon, Mr. R. R. Knight, took a very great interest in this question and on a number of occasions moved a similar bill.

I would think that any piece of literature which was put out by the company, or any advertising in newspapers which set forth repayment schedules would, according to this bill, have to have included in it the interest rates that are charged.
I think there is evidence that small loans companies in their enthusiasm to make loans and their enthusiasm to make profits do put forward literature which paints an exceedingly rosy picture as far as the borrower is concerned, and I think it should have coupled with it a statement setting forth what are the interest rates. I have in my hand a brochure passed out to prospective borrowers by the Beneficial Finance Company which says, inside the cover, the following:
Dear Customer:
We are happy to offer you the full services of the Beneficial Finance System.
Your Beneficial manager and his staff are carefully trained and thoroughly experienced to give friendly, intelligent service in all matters of personal finance, budgets, and loans. Feel free to call on them at any time.
No doubt hon. members will have heard advertisements over the radio. Some of them go something like this: come in some morning.

Frank is a fine fellow, used to dealing with the public. You won't have to have any embarrassing co-signatures, and you can get your loan in a matter of minutes. However, the experience of many people with regard to small loans companies suggests that their interest rates are so high that there should be in their advertising the interest rates that are being charged. This pamphlet goes on to say-incidentally, there is a big heading:
"You're the boss" at Beneficial.
I do not imagine that is really correct, by the way, even when you are borrowing money. I am certain it is not correct if you are in default and unable to make your payments on time. It goes on to say:
Extra Cash
Even though you already have a loan with us, you can get more cash at any time by "adding it on" to your present account... Just phone and tell the manager how much cash you want. He'll save you time ... he'll have the paper-work done before you come in to pick up your loan.
You will not even have to take the time to read it. He will have it all ready for you. And again:
Bill Clean-up Service
Pay off left-over bills with a bill clean-up loan. Then, make only one monthly payment instead of several.. . have more cash left over at the end of the month.
It goes on:
Consideration
Naturally, we like prompt repayments. However, in an emergency, if you can't make a payment, let us know and we'll do everything possible to help straighten things out.
That is the Beneficial Finance Company. They say that if a customer cannot make payments on time, let them know and they will do everything possible to straighten things out.
I have in my hand a copy of the chattel mortgage which is signed when a customer enters into an agreement with the Beneficial Finance Company, and I should like to read a paragraph from that chattel mortgage:
And it is agreed that in case default shall be made in the payment of the sum of money in the said proviso mentioned or of the cost of loans and interest after default or any part thereof as hereinbefore provided or in case the mortgagee feels unsafe or insecure or deems such goods and chattels in danger of being sold or removed-
That is, if the Beneficial Finance Company should feel unsafe or insecure
__then the whole of the money secured hereby
shall at the option of the mortgagee immediately become due and payable-
Notice, that if the company feels insecure the mortgage is due and payable.
-and it shall be lawful for the mortgagee, its servant or servants, with such assistance as he or they may require at any time during the day or

Those words are contained in a chattel mortgage that has been signed. It states that the company has the right to hire what I call a gang of thugs-

No, but I am suggesting the house has jurisdiction over interest rates. In this bill I am suggesting that this house has jurisdiction over advertising. I am not a lawyer but I would think this house because of its jurisdiction over small loans companies could exercise at least a measure of persuasion when it comes to advertising to see to it that the advertising is not as misleading as I contend this is when, in reference to failure to make prompt payments, the Beneficial Finance Company states in its brochure:
Consideration-Naturally, we like prompt repayments. However, in an emergency, if you can't make a payment, let us know and we'll do everything possible to help straighten things out.
I should think you would be better off if you did not let them know because it might give them this feeling of insecurity and might
Small Loans Act
lead to the adoption by them of these strong-arm methods to break into your house by day or by night, singly or in groups, to seize the chattels in question.
I believe hon. members of the house are sympathetic to the idea that in advertising there should be the utmost measure of modesty and that with respect to advertising dealing with repayments and charges thereon a company should set forth the interest rates they are charging so the public will have access to all the facts.
In recent years the period the house devotes to the discussion of public bills has not been used to the greatest advantage. There has been too great a tendency to talk out many public bills that are placed on the order paper, if indeed not all of them. I would hope that before this session concludes this bill will come to a vote. I should like to see it referred to the banking and commerce committee and the superintendent of insurance for whom I have respect and who has my confidence called as a witness before that committee so that hon. members could judge whether it is in the public interest to take this small but important step of requiring small loans companies to state in their literature and advertising the actual percentage of interest they charge on repayments.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments on the bill as presented to this house.
First, I would agree with the hon. member that it is advisable that the matter should be discussed in this house but I would be quick to point out that the legislation in its present form does not really hit at those who are abusing the privilege of advertising. It is, in effect, restrictive, and somewhat prejudices those companies that are now under control, namely companies that lend under $1,500. In my opinion the greatest abuse of this practice comes about through individuals and companies who are not even within the control of any statute. For that reason I feel that the hon. member is putting companies which are now under control at an unfair advantage. I believe, too, he is placing over those companies control of a kind that is not even put over the lending operations of the banks, such as the personal loans branch of the Canadian Bank of Commerce. That, of course, may not be an effective argument in reply to the hon. member.

subtopic: AMENDMENT REQUIRING STATEMENT OF TRUE INTEREST RATE CHARGED
speechtext: There are several banks that follow that plan now in addition to the Canadian Bank of Commerce.

subtopic: AMENDMENT REQUIRING STATEMENT OF TRUE INTEREST RATE CHARGED
speechtext:
Yes, that is true. The banks that have followed that plan would not be under the jurisdiction of this legislation.
In 1957 the hire and purchase act was passed in Great Britain which indirectly attempted to deal with this problem. It dealt with the buying of goods and chattels on time. That measure required that the exact terms of such purchases be set out in the advertisements. Of course, as we know, these agreements are usually assigned to finance companies at a discount and thus would apply indirectly to the principle set out in the bill before us.
We are somewhat handicapped in this country in bringing these matters directly under control because we fall between the jurisdiction of this parliament over interest and the jurisdiction of the provinces over matters of contract, over mortgages, chattel mortgages, and so forth. I question whether the matter of costs, as dealt with here, could be dealt with by this house because it may be a matter of contract between the person who is negotiating the loan and the company. I think when the Small Loans Act was brought before the house before and which dealt with the cost of interest it was only done so with the consent of the provinces concerned to give it effect, and that would have to be obtained in this case. However, Mr. Speaker, I think that in bringing this before the house

the hon. member has given us perhaps an opportunity of discussing the merits or otherwise of advertising by finance companies.
Of course, in a competitive society we must use some discretion in our control of advertising. As was discussed in a measure earlier, we must, I think, examine the advertising and ask whether it is misleading the public. If it is misleading the public, then perhaps it could be dealt with either by the Criminal Code or by some specific legislation; but I think the whole matter points out the fact that there is a field in financing over $1,500 that comes somewhat between the jurisdiction of this parliament and of the provincial governments in the control of second mortgages, and so on, on which there have been large profits and which perhaps have been draining off money from the main channel of finance, and if it were brought back in under more reasonable rates it would add to the flow of money in legitimate commercial fields and perhaps help to keep down the interest rate.
Recently in Toronto Pierre Berton made an expose of an advertising scheme of a company which operated under four different names and had various forms of advertising in the local papers setting out how easy it was to obtain money, that there were no hidden costs and various things such as the regular come-ons similar to the advertising read out by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue).
In his column in the Toronto Star of October 8, 1959, Pierre Berton showed how this worked. I do not feel that I should disclose names in this forum at this time because I have not been able to verify that this story is correct, but unofficially I know it has been checked. I have seen documentation of it. I will relate the story as follows. This lady was in difficulties financially; a third mortgage was due. She required money to pay it off and other financing, and she read the advertisement:
I'll lend you $1,525 to $5,000 within three hours.
The advertisement carried a photograph of a businessman, as these advertisements often do. They keep changing the names and this man, as I understand it, had really nothing to do with this business. They were sort of fronts to give some suggestion of being reputable. She made an application and they asked her if she would bring in her papers so that they would check over her documents to see whether she owned the property or not. Their initial statement was, if you receive $1,525 you will repay $30.84 monthly, the time being for 60 months. If you calculate that you will see she was paying interest at about a rate of 7.8 per cent per annum, and that did not seem unreasonable, in view of

the other financial costs of obtaining mortgages, and particularly third mortgages, in the city of Toronto.
But what happened? When she went back she was told that if she signed a document acknowledging that she had received the loan but there would be no hold on her property. She asked if she needed legal advice and she was told, "No, you do not need legal advice; we provide that for you gratis as part of the service." When she went to leave they gave her a cheque for $574.20. She was told that was the difference between the money she had borrowed and the amount they had used to pay off her mortgage. When she got home and worked it out she found she had been short-changed about $109. She complained about that and she was given the $109 after an apology. There were various charges on it, and she received a total of $1,516.50. When she got the document back that she had signed she found she had signed for $2,225 at 12 per cent interest. This was not in the contract. This was one of those things that was not supposed to be a hidden charge. This is what the poor lady had to sign and her monthly payment was $35. The interest was calculated half yearly.
The agreement was to fall due in four years. In four years anyone who has any knowledge of figures, of course, would figure out that she would have owed the company about $1,580, which was $65 more than she owed when she started, and all during this period of years she would have paid off about $1,680. Now, this is not only unfair but it is deceptive advertising. True she was 21, and she went in there on her own will. She should have had advice. She was misled; but it seems to me this is the type of advertising that the hon. member is referring to, and yet it is not controlled by this act, and this is the field in which most of the abuse is being carried out.
After this expose the company promised to change its tactics. It did change its name, and I believe it is still operating. How many people are going to be fooled by this type of
Business of the House
advertising until some sort of protection can be given? I do not believe we can be too restrictive on the type of advertising that is used. We must give some free play in free enterprise for advertising goods, but I believe there are occasions, such as I have indicated here, where there has been, I was going to say, deceit and misleading of people who are in difficulty, who are burdened with debt and as such perhaps cannot afford to get the advice that they feel they should get. For that reason I feel, although the principle of the bill is good, it is not adequate to meet the problem at hand.
